lead: When every generator is offline and no APU or ground power is connected, the battery is the source left; it carries the essential loads until another source comes on line. A 24 V lead-acid battery has 12 cells of about 2 V. A 24 V nickel-cadmium battery has 19 or 20 cells of about 1.2 V. Newer aircraft also fly lithium-ion batteries. Aircraft use batteries for engine and APU starting, the emergency DC bus and standby instruments. Some syllabi cover the chemistry and testing only briefly; the comparison is examined everywhere.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 and Chapter 3.2, because the battery sits on the DC bus and is charged through a TRU or dedicated charger.

sections.h3: Lead-acid: 12 cells, sulphuric acid, specific gravity

blocks.text: A lead-acid cell has a lead-dioxide positive plate, a sponge-lead negative plate and dilute sulphuric acid electrolyte. Each cell is about 2.1 V on open circuit and about 2 V on load; twelve in series make the 24 V battery. Specific gravity near 1.28 at full charge shows state of charge, because charging raises acid concentration. Read it after the battery rests or after mixing; water added during topping up lowers the reading until it mixes.

Lead-acid gives strong cranking current and is cheap, but heavy per ampere-hour. Deep discharge damages the plates. Capacity is in ampere-hours (Ah): Ah = I × t, where I is current in amperes and t is time in hours. C-rate = I ÷ rated Ah; a 40 Ah battery at 40 A is 1C, the 1-hour rate. Lead-acid voltage falls steadily during discharge, so the end point is easy to see.

sections.h3: Nickel-cadmium: 19 or 20 cells, flat voltage, thermal risk

blocks.text: A nickel-cadmium (NiCd) cell uses nickel hydroxide positive and cadmium negative plates in potassium hydroxide electrolyte. Sintered plates pack active material into a porous nickel matrix. Each cell gives about 1.2 V, so 20 cells give 24 V and 19 cells about 22.8 V; both are sold as 24 V batteries. Never use a 12-cell lead-acid charger setting on a NiCd battery.

NiCd has low internal resistance, good cold performance and long life. Its voltage stays almost flat until nearly discharged, so a simple voltage reading is a poor state-of-charge check. NiCd is prone to thermal runaway on a constant-voltage charge: as the cells warm, their voltage falls, so the charger pushes more current, which heats them further until electrolyte boils off or a cell vents. Battery temperature sensors and a charger that limits current stop this. NiCd also shows voltage depression, often called memory effect, after repeated shallow cycling; a full discharge and recharge in the battery shop restores most capacity.

A capacity check discharges the battery at constant current to a stated end voltage (about 1.0 V per NiCd cell), records the ampere-hours removed and compares them with the rated Ah; Worked example 2 does one. Lead-acid charges at constant current, then at constant voltage (float) to avoid overcharge. Nickel-cadmium is charged at constant current, stopped by voltage or temperature cut-off. Never leave a NiCd on a constant-voltage charge, for the reason above. Deep discharge below the end voltage damages both types.

Depth of discharge (DoD) = (Ah removed ÷ rated Ah) × 100 %. In Worked example 1, 20 Ah from a 40 Ah battery is 50 % DoD. The remaining 20 Ah at 20 A lasts 1 hour if rate effects are ignored; at high current the usable capacity is lower.

Lithium-ion cells are about 3.6 to 3.7 V each, so far fewer cells are needed for a 28 V DC system: the B787 main and APU batteries have eight cells in series. Lithium-ion stores more energy per kilogram than lead-acid or NiCd and keeps a flatter voltage, but a cell that is overcharged, over-discharged or damaged can go into thermal runaway and set its neighbours alight. So every lithium battery has a battery management system (BMS) that watches each cell voltage and temperature, balances the cells and cuts charging off. In January 2013 two B787 battery thermal-runaway events grounded the fleet for about three months; the fix added cell insulation, a sealed steel case and a vent line that takes any smoke overboard. Lithium iron phosphate cells, which are harder to drive into runaway, now replace NiCd in some emergency and standby batteries.

examples.question: A 24 V lead-acid battery is rated 40 Ah at the 1-hour rate. It supplies 40 A for 30 minutes. (a) How many ampere-hours are used? (b) What is the depth of discharge? (c) If the load then drops to 20 A, how long will the remaining charge last?
steps: Ah used = I × t = 40 A × 0.5 h = 20 Ah.
examples.answer: 20 Ah is used, the depth of discharge is 50%, and the remaining charge lasts 1 hour at 20 A, ignoring rate effects.

examples.question: A 24 V, 40 Ah nickel-cadmium battery with 20 cells is given a capacity check. It is discharged at the 1-hour rate and reaches the end voltage of 1.0 V per cell after 51 minutes. (a) What is the discharge current and the end voltage of the battery? (b) What capacity did it deliver, as Ah and as a percentage of its rating?
steps: (a) The 1-hour rate of a 40 Ah battery is 40 A (1C).
examples.answer: It was discharged at 40 A to 20 V and delivered 34 Ah, 85 % of its rating. The shop compares this with the limit in the battery's maintenance manual; a low result calls for a deep-cycle reconditioning and a second check.

traps: Do not assume a 24 V NiCd battery has 12 cells; it has 19 or 20 cells.
Do not take a specific-gravity reading just after topping up with water; the acid is diluted until mixing.
Do not read 40 Ah as a continuous 40 A rating; it is 40 A for 1 hour at the 1-hour rate.
Do not call every NiCd capacity loss memory effect; ageing, dry-out and overcharge also reduce capacity, which is why a timed capacity check is used.
Do not use open-circuit voltage alone for NiCd state of charge; its curve is flat.

quiz.q: How many cells make a 24 V lead-acid and a 24 V NiCd battery?
quiz.a: 12 lead-acid cells of about 2 V; 19 or 20 NiCd cells of about 1.2 V.

quiz.q: Why is specific gravity used on lead-acid batteries?
quiz.a: It indicates state of charge because charging changes acid concentration; near 1.28 means full charge.

quiz.q: A 30 Ah battery at the 1-hour rate supplies 15 A for 48 minutes. Find Ah used and depth of discharge.
Explain thermal runaway in a NiCd battery.
quiz.a: On a constant-voltage charge, a warm NiCd cell's voltage falls, so the charger drives more current; the current heats the cell further and the loop runs away until electrolyte boils off or the cell vents. Temperature sensing and a current-limited charge stop it.
Discharge current divided by rated Ah; 40 A from a 40 Ah battery is 1C.

quiz.q: Why is terminal voltage a poor NiCd state-of-charge check?
quiz.a: Its voltage stays almost flat until nearly empty, so a small voltage change covers a large capacity change.

quiz.q: Why does an aircraft lithium-ion battery need a battery management system?
quiz.a: Each cell must stay inside its voltage and temperature window; overcharge, over-discharge or damage can start thermal runaway that spreads to the next cell. The BMS monitors and balances each cell and cuts the charge off.

beyond: Not for the exam. Battery management systems now estimate state of health from current, voltage and temperature, not from specific gravity. Certification of lithium batteries now includes tests that one cell in runaway does not spread to its neighbours. Search for battery management system, state of health and thermal runaway propagation next.
